comparison: Both strongly support the experimental design (C3-C6, C35, C39-C42). OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment including controls, replication, and statistical power. Peer reviewers accept the design as 'state-of-the-art' and appropriate for the research question. Complete agreement on experimental validity.

Both support the main finding of weak evidence for selection on induced epigenetic variation (C7-C8, C45-C46, C50, C68, C71). OpenEval emphasizes the statistical rigor and appropriate interpretation of small effect sizes. Peer reviewers unanimously accept this as a 'convincing negative result' and treat it as the primary finding. Strong concordance.

Both accept the statistical analysis of phenotypic variation sources (C43-C44, C61-C64, C67). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of statistical methods and effect size quantification. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as supporting context for the main negative result. Agreement on statistical framework.

Both strongly support the methylation analysis findings (C47-C49, C77-C78, C86). OpenEval details the methodological soundness (WGBS, sample size, filtering, FDR correction) and appropriate interpretation of minimal differential methylation. Peer reviewers accept this as part of 'state-of-the-art' methods contributing to the convincing negative result. Complete agreement.

Both support the molecular characterization including GO enrichment (C84-C85). OpenEval notes methodological soundness while appropriately cautioning about biological significance given small DMC numbers. Peer reviewers accept these details as supporting evidence for minimal epigenetic differentiation. Agreement with similar interpretive caution.

Both accept the detailed molecular characterization of DMCs (C79, C81-C83). OpenEval evaluates the technical aspects of the methylation analysis. Peer reviewers treat this as part of the comprehensive molecular evidence supporting the negative result. Concordance on technical validity.

Both support the findings and interpretation of maternal line effects and data quality issues (C69-C70, C72-C73, plus C9 and C66 in peer review). OpenEval praises the transparency and critical self-evaluation. Peer reviewers accept the authors' caveats and agree these don't represent strong evidence for epigenetic selection. Strong agreement on interpretation.

Partial overlap on maternal line effects (C9). OpenEval focuses on the logical framework for interpreting maternal effects (C9, C65, C67, C100). Peer R9 includes C9 along with data quality concerns (C66, C69-C70, C72-C73). Both accept the findings but peer review groups with quality control issues while OpenEval treats interpretation separately.

Minimal overlap on C67 (maternal line interpretation). OpenEval R6 focuses on maternal line effects framework. Peer R4 addresses statistical findings about phenotypic variation. Both support their respective claims but address largely different aspects of the analysis.

Both strongly support the reanalysis identifying experimental error in Lin et al. 2024 (C11-C12, C54-C56, C89-C92, C97-C98). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of the genetic distance analysis and variant calling methodology. Peer reviewers unanimously find this 'convincing' evidence of mix-ups, with one suggesting retraction of the 2024 paper. Complete agreement that this is a major contribution.

Both support the quantitative genetic evidence from the reanalysis (C93-C96). OpenEval emphasizes the compelling visual and quantitative evidence from genetic distance analysis. Peer reviewers accept these distance metrics as convincing proof of experimental error. Strong concordance on the strength of this evidence.

Partial overlap on reanalysis conclusions (C10, C51-C52). OpenEval R7 focuses on the technical reanalysis methodology and findings. Peer R8 emphasizes the broader conclusion about weak evidence (C60) and contrast with Lin et al. Both support the findings but peer review focuses more on the interpretive significance for the field.

Both strongly support the main conclusions (C57-C59). OpenEval finds the conclusions appropriately cautious and well-supported, particularly the distinction between standing and induced variation. Peer reviewers accept the nuanced conclusion and view the negative results as 'important' for clarifying the limited role of induced epigenetic variation. Complete agreement.

Both support the overall conclusion of weak evidence (C60). OpenEval synthesizes findings from both the current study and reanalysis. Peer reviewers emphasize this as an 'important, clarifying contribution' in a controversial field. Strong agreement on the significance and validity of the negative result.

OpenEval supports claims about prior work context (C29-C34, C109-C111), including appropriate self-criticism about potential residual heterozygosity in Schmid et al. 2018b. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific contextual claims about previous studies.

OpenEval supports the background and literature review claims (C1-C2, C13-C28) as accurately representing the field and providing appropriate context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background claims.

OpenEval supports the literature synthesis and mechanistic discussion (C99, C112-C118), particularly regarding mitotic versus meiotic inheritance differences. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific discussion points.

OpenEval supports the methodological discussion and future research suggestions (C101-C102, C105-C108, C119), including recommendations to study species with different reproductive modes. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these forward-looking suggestions.
